Beneath
be-NEETH
prep., adv.
Old English beneothan, below. Webster 1828: under; lower in place; also, lower in rank, dignity, or excellence. In the Authorized Version it draws the vertical axis of the universe — heaven above, earth beneath, the water under the earth — and our Lord uses it to divide two orders of men.

Biblical Definition

Beneath in Scripture is first cosmological and then moral. The second commandment maps the whole created order with it: Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth (Exodus 20:4). Nothing in any tier of creation may be made into an image of God, which is the point of the exhaustive survey. Deuteronomy repeats the tiers when it forbids the likeness of any fish that is in the waters beneath the earth (Deuteronomy 4:18). The tabernacle uses the word technically, of boards coupled together beneath at the corners (Exodus 26:24) and of the brasen grate under the compass of the altar beneath unto the midst of it (Exodus 38:4). Then the Lord Jesus takes the vertical axis and makes it a division of persons: Ye are from beneath; I am from above: ye are of this world; I am not of this world (John 8:23). That is not geography. It is origin, nature, and destiny, and it is the plainest statement in the Gospels that the difference between Christ and unbelieving men is not degree but source.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BENEATH as under; lower in place; and figuratively, lower in rank, dignity, or excellence — also, unworthy of, as beneath a man’s notice. The KJV uses the literal sense throughout and the figurative in John 8:23.

expand to see more

BENEATH, prep. — Under; lower in place, with something directly over or on; as, the earth beneath our feet.

Lower in rank, dignity or excellence; as, brutes are beneath man.

Unbecoming; unworthy of; as, an action beneath a gentleman.

BENEATH, adv. — In a lower place; below, as opposed to heaven or to any thing above.

Webster’s adverbial gloss — below, as opposed to heaven — is precisely the contrast our Lord draws in John 8:23.

Key Scripture

Exodus 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:"

Deuteronomy 4:18 — "The likeness of any thing that creepeth on the ground, the likeness of any fish that is in the waters beneath the earth:"

Exodus 26:24 — "And they shall be coupled together beneath, and they shall be coupled together above the head of it unto one ring: thus shall it be for them both; they shall be for the two corners."

Exodus 38:4 — "And he made for the altar a brasen grate of network under the compass thereof beneath unto the midst of it."

John 8:23 — "And he said unto them, Ye are from beneath; I am from above: ye are of this world; I am not of this world."

Modern Corruption

John 8:23 is corrupted whenever the division between from beneath and from above is softened into a difference of maturity, temperament, or spiritual journey rather than a difference of origin and nature.

expand to see more

Our Lord’s sentence admits no middle tier. Ye are from beneath; I am from above is spoken to religious men, not to obvious reprobates, and it locates the problem below their behaviour, in their source. The doctrine is total depravity and the necessity of the new birth: Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God (John 3:3). Preaching that treats the unconverted as Christians at an earlier stage — further back on the same road — has erased the vertical line John 8:23 draws. There is no gradual ascent from beneath to above; there is a birth from above, and it is God’s to give.

The second commandment’s use of the word guards a related truth. God forbids the likeness of anything in heaven above, in the earth beneath, or in the water under the earth — the survey is exhaustive precisely because human ingenuity is. Every tier of creation has been tried as material for an image, and every one is refused. Where the modern instinct wants a God who can be pictured, felt, and localized — whether in a statue, an experience, or a screen — Exodus 20:4 has already ruled on the whole class. The regulative principle of worship stands on this verse: God is to be worshipped as He has commanded, and no image of any tier of creation may stand in for Him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew is tachath, under or beneath, the ordinary preposition of what lies below; the Greek in John 8:23 is kato, below, set against ano, above.

expand to see more

Hebrew tachath (H8478) — under, beneath, in place of; the ordinary preposition of position below (Exodus 20:4; Deuteronomy 4:18).

Hebrew mattah (H4295) — downward, beneath; used of the lower part of a structure (Exodus 26:24; 38:4).

Greek kato (G2736) — below, downward; ye are from beneath (John 8:23).

Greek ano (G507) — above; the contrasting term in the same verse and in Colossians 3:1-2, seek those things which are above.

The threefold cosmology of Exodus 20:4 — heaven above, earth beneath, water under the earth — is a merism for the whole creation, not a scientific diagram.

Usage

"In the earth beneath (Exodus 20:4) — one tier of an exhaustive survey; no part of creation may be made an image of God."

"Coupled together beneath (Exodus 26:24) — the technical builder’s sense in the tabernacle."

"Ye are from beneath; I am from above (John 8:23) — origin, not degree; the line the new birth crosses."
